maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Minister of Customs and Excise) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 237, to amend the Petroleum and Naphtha Inspection Act.

maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If hon. members will look at the bill they will see that the measure speaks for itself. The amendments proposed are indicated in italics. The object of the proposed change is to permit the sale of naphtha. Under the present act the Governor in Council can regulate the possession, storage and transportation of naphtha and its sale is restricted except for certain purposes. In its present form the act reads:
Naphtha shall not be sold or offered for sale in Canada for illuminating purposes except,-
(a)	for use in street lamps in which only the vapour is burned; or
(b)	for use in dwellings, factories and other places of business when vapourized in secure underground tanks outside the buildings in which the vapour so generated is used for lighting.
We want to make regulations so that the sale will be permitted for lighting purposes. This is rendered necessary by the invention of the Coleman lamp which has been put on the market and is going into general use. Doubtless hon. members are all familiar with the Coleman lamp. The insurance companies and the best experts in the United States have declared that it is perfectly safe. As the law now stands, a dealer or a man who has naphtha in his possession cannot sell it for illuminating purposes except as restricted by the general statute. The purpose of the present bill is to permit the sale of naphtha for illuminating purposes under regulations to be made by the Governor in Council.

Dairy Industry Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I will
promise my hon. friend that it will not be brought up before Tuesday.

Can we get an explanation
of this from the minister?

This whole resolution was associated with the Dairy Industry Act, which was discharged from the Order Paper two or three weeks ago, with one important difference, that difference being in clause 2 which we are now discussing. The reason that I have incorporated this clause in the present resolution and did not have it in the resolution when it was previously before the House, is this. Last year when the discussion was up on the oleomargarine question, I took the ground that, in my opinion, a better solution of the question of a cheap spread for bread was renovated butter and not oleomargarine. Last year the House did not take my statement very seriously, and as the question was not before the House, I suppose they were justified in assuming that attitude. At the same time I gave my assurance that if the oleomargarine resolution met with the same decision last year as it has this year, I would immediately advise my colleagues that in my estimation it would be
a good idea to remove the prohibition on the manufacture of renovated butter. Inasmuch, however, as the vote of the House last year was in favour of continuing the manufacture of oleomargarine, there was no call for such action. This year I had no occasion to make any remarks with regard to the question of oleomargarine, as the matter seemed to be in a fairly good condition, and I was afraid that possibly I might spoil it by saying anything. Nevertheless, had I said anything, I would have re-stated my position as regards renovated butter as a cheap bread spread for the poor man. I feel calleid upon to implement that pledge of last year. I will read from Hansard just one extract indicating what I said, and I will not read any more than is necessary. I said:
I am prepared, if my colleagues will agree with me, to take that prohibition off by legislation this session-
That was last session.
-as a means of giving real relief; as a means of giving butter which is not 2 per cent butter-some of my friends here claim that they have had enough 2 per cent-but 100 per cent butter with 100 per cent food content.
That was ray statement last year and although I did not repeat it in the House for the reasons I have indicated, I have repeated it in letters to various individuals throughout Canada. I stated to these parties that I recognized that there was an argument in favour of some kind of cheap spread for bread for people who could not-or felt that they could	not-afford	to buy
creamery butter; that inasmuch as oleomargarine was a commodity of which nobody knew the ingredients, it was, in my estimation defective in food properties. As the House has decided to revert to the old order of things by a resolution passed recently, I am here to carry out my statement as regards the manufacture of renovated butter.
As this is a comparatively new question, the people of Canada do not know much about renovated butter. It has been prohibited for twenty years, and because it has been prohibited for so long it is a comparatively new question to possibly ninety-five per cent of the people. What is this new article and what is the history of its prohibition? In order to give an answer to that question, we have in this resolution and in a bill associated with it, merely asked that the Governor in Council be given power by proclamation to provide for the manufacture of this product. It is not proposed to authorize this immediately. A period will elapse, to be determined by the amount of requests for the manufacture of renovated butter. If nobody

Dairy Industry Act
calls for the manufacture of it, if the labour organizations, the women's organizations, the miners' organizations, the lumber organizations, and any others, make no requests, the chances are that no proclamation will be issued, inasmuch as this would indicate that there was no demand.
Why am I bringing in this bill? In the first place, because I want to carry out my statement; and, secondly, because I believe there is room in our domestic economy for such a product as renovated butter. The question is a considerable one that presents many phases, and later on, if the discussion is protracted, I may find it necessary to deal with some of the details. In the meantime my primary object is to meet a demand which I am convinced exists. There has been some criticism with regard to the question of importation. Some critics take the ground that there would be no objection to providing a market for the dairy butter made by the pioneer settler, by putting it into proper shape to be sold before it deteriorated to too great an extent. It sometimes happens that butter shipped to an outside market becomes bad when it is a long time in transit; occasionally it is not shipped in refrigerator cars, and by the time it reaches Minneapolis, say, or New York, it is in a worse condition than renovated butter manufactured and sold on the Canadian market. There is the assurance, ns embodied in the resolution, that the manufacture of renovated butter will be legal only upon the issuance of a proclamation; and personally I would not mind incorporating in the bill a provision that no such proclamation should be issued within a year, or at least until there was an evident demand from those most concerned. I want to assure the committee that I have no desire whatever to thrust anything like this upon the market if there is no demand for it; but there is undoubtedly a certain amount of demand on the part of the wholesale produce dealers who handle our dairy butter. People have repeatedly written to me, particularly from the West, wanting to know, inasmuch as this article is produced by farmers, and was the only kind of butter we had fifty years ago, why it should be banished from the country in summary fashion, having to climb a tariff wall of eight cents a pound to get into the United States. It is further pointed out that the local country stores experience considerable difficulty in finding a market for it. It is urged that provision should be made for the manufacture of it in Canada, and I think it may very reasonably be inferred from all the circumstances that there is at least suffi-

cient demand to warrant the action we propose taking. The night the oleomargarine debate concluded, about ten days ago, some hon. gentlemen asked me why I did not bring down a measure with regard to renovated butter; and one person particularly pointed out that inasmuch as the poor people weie going to be deprived of oleomargarine there was no reason why this other substitute, or rather this form of butter, should not be manufactured. That, Mr. Chairman, is briefly a summary of the situation. I may remark, by the way, that I have referred the matter to my colleagues who have agreed to the proposal, believing it to be a good one.
Will the minister explain to the committee how renovated butter is made? What is the composition of it? Is it defined?

I have been trying to ascertain the quality of the product during the past five or six years; in fact, before coming here at all I was interested in the subject. The moment that the manufacture of oleomargarine was permitted there immediately arose the question why this product should be banished from the market. I have had some correspondence with American manufacturers in reference to this matter, and one letter that I have received is particularly interesting. I shall not read the whole of the letter because I think it is rather too long to put on Hansard. But it is from ao authority in Chicago, a man who, I may say, is not a manufacturer of renovated butter but a real dairyman whose interests are rather, if anything, opposed to this product. Still inasmuch as renovated butter is a recognized and standard article on the market, being quoted just the same as creamery butter, it is well that there should be no misapprehension regarding its nature and value. Renovated butter is usually quoted about halfway between creamery butter and oleomargarine. About a fortnight ago oleomargarine let us say, stood at 30 cents-I am not giving the exact figures, of course, but the proportions are true-while creamery butter was quoted at 40 cents. Renovated butter then would fetch 4 cents more than oleomargarine and 6 cents less than creamery butter. Sometimes the variation is exactly midway between the two extremes of oleomargarine and creamery butter. The letter to which I have referred comes from Mr. G. L. McKay, secretary of the American Association of Creamery Butter Manufacturers. It is not addressed to me personally, because I am not acquainted with Mr. McKay, but my department is constantly in touch with the organization of which Mr. McKay is

Dairy Industry Act
secretary, and the letter from which I am about to quote was written to Mr. J. A. Ruddick, the Dairy and Cold Storage Commissioner. Mr. McKay gives a good deal more information than we asked for, but it is all very interesting. We merely inquired, by telegram, the value of renovated butter as a food product as compared with butter and other articles: we were anxious to know what part these mysterious vitamines played in this particular foodstuff. Mr. McKay says: There is nothing about renovated butter that should make it in any way unwholesome. Ladles or farm butter is gathered together and melted at a moderate heat. The pure butterfat or oil is pumped from the melting vat into funnel shaped tanks and air is blown through it, and that removes any odours that may adhere to the fat.
I may explain here that one of the reasons why dairy butter does not always keep is the fact that it is salted with exceedingly coarse salt, and often there is too much water left in it. Frequently, too, an excess of buttermilk or curd is left in the butter and its keeping properties are consequently impaired, so that it becomes rancid if not kept in cold storage.
When the oil becomes odourless it runs into cold water where it goes back into butter flakes, looking very much like butter granules. A starter is added to this,-
Sometimes people take this word "starter" to indicate a chemical compound, but it is nothing more nor less than sour cream. It is put into the churn to promote acidity. Seldom do we find dairy butter made from entirely sweet milk; there is always a slight acidity to it.
-and the granules in the same conditions stay in the starter for some time, and it is then worked in the usual manner. Some pour the starter into the oil, X understand, before it runs into the water to be congealed:	in other words, renovated butter is butter
that has not been made right on the farm. It contains too much salt, or too much water, or too much curd. It is usually churned at too high a temperature and contains a lot of curd. Coarse salt is frequently used, and butter of a poor character is the result.
I will venture the suggestion, without knowing much about the business of some of my hon. friends opposite, that they have often been tempted themselves to raise the temperature of cream to make it "come."

Does the
minister speak from experience?
I do.
Might that remark be considered a reflection on members on this side?

Not at all; I think it ought to be taken as a compliment. If hon. gentlemen are not familiar with these
things, then there is something lacking in their agricultural knowledge. Mr. McKay says:
The business has gone back in this country-
That is, the United States.
-very much due to the fact there are not as many farmers now making their own butter. The centralized system has extended so much in our country and covers such a wide territory and cream is shipped such a long distance that the farmers that used to make their own butter and trade it for groceries are selling their cream to the centralizers. Cream buying stations are scattered all over tihe United States. The farmer now brings in his cream in a crock or pail if he only has two or three cows, and if he has more he brings it in a can. It is only in scattered districts that the farmer is still making butter.
As far as purity goes, I can see no reason but what renovated butter is as clean and pure as any butter that is made.
As hon. gentlemen know, it depends on the buttermaker. I think half the people of Canada would prefer dairy butter if they could get it of good quality. In many instances they can and do get a good quality, because the product of a home dairy, made from one herd, under the supervision of one person who is a capable buttermaker, is at least quite equal to the average creamery butter.
I have seen some of it that would score 94 or 95. This depends somewhat upon the quality of the raw material, or the quality of the butter that was melted and the manner of making it. In scoring contests I have run across it several times put in as creamery butter. I invariably have been able to detect it by letting it dissolve in my mouth.
One of the reasons why renovated butter was prohibited was not because of its quality generally, but because those in charge of the dairy industry at that time were afraid that it might be mixed with creamery butter and jeopardize our market in the United Kingdom. Since then, however, we have instituted a grading system, so that this objection does not apply to-day as it did twenty years ago.
There is a slight oily taste. Then if it is broken apart on the trier, the grain is rather fine and glistens a little more than the ordinary creamery butter.
The word "grain" is not used very much now; we speak of "texture".
I talked with Mr. W. S. Moore, commission merchant, who used to be head of a large process factory, after receiving your telegram.
It used to be called "process butter".
He recommended it very highly although he is not dealing in it at the present time. He said that he has bought as much as ten or twelve carloads of ladle butter from northwest Canada a year, and he thinks in a country where there are a lot of farmers butter made especially of an irregular quality that a renovated factory would be a good thing.
In the wire sent to this gentleman there was no suggestion that we wanted information of this kind. Apparently in view of the situation
Dairy Industry Act

in the United States he wondered why Canada did not renovate its homemade butter. Thi3 is a long letter and I do not think I need read any further.
During the debate on oleomargarine the trouble feared seemed to be the mixing of butter with oleo. Is there any danger in this case of the mixing of oleomargarine with butter?

I do not anticipate any danger from oleomargarine inasmuch as the right to manufacture it will expire in August and it cannot be offered for sale after March next. But there is a danger of this renovated butter being mixed with creamery butter, and therefore if its manufacture is permitted it will have to be subject to the stipulation that it be manufactured in an entirely separate building, so there will not be the least temptation to work it into creamery butter. That is the danger which exists to-day with regard to oleomargarine. As a matter of fact "manna" consists of oleo mixed with butter. This bill prohibits the mixing of any foreign fats with butter. It provides that butter shall consist of eighty per cent butter fat, and this leaves no room for foreign fats as the other 20 per cent consists of salt and water.
Where does the minister expect to get a market for the renovated butter?

Very much the same market that oleomargarine now supplies-those who want a cheap spread. In the United States renovated butter is made of such a generally high standard that the market is not confined to the poorer people, the price being within six cents of creamery butter. I hope the committee, Mr. Chairman, will not look upon me as an ardent advocate of the use of inferior butter. I am not anxious to press renovated butter upon an unwilling country. I simply want to redeem my promise that this opportunity of obtaining a cheap spread would be given.
As a pioneer in Manitoba, I am sure the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) must have made a considerable amount of butter. I can recall the time, too, when the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Hopkins) was a trail blazer in improving dairying in the old Northwest Territories. They will remember that at that time there was nothing but dairy butter made; and this has always been the case with our early settlers. At the present time, the surplus of our dairy butter after supplying the home requirements has to get over the eight-eent American tariff wall and the handicap of express and freight charges. The result is that the price paid to 
the frontier man is very very small, especially since the Fordney tariff went into force. Consequently this is one of the advantages of introducing renovated butter at this time if the people want it-a home market will be provided. Nobody is going to force renovated butter on the people; and that is why we want an educative campaign throughout the country. The people do not understand what renovated butter is. It is simply the dairy butter that most of us were brought up on, which, having become rancid, is put in a condition fit for food. I am sure that any pioneer in Canada who had to keep the wolf from the door, as I and many others did, by making dairy butter, will have compassion upon the frontier man who still relies on his output of dairy butter during the summer for his grocery supplies. It is an advantage that works both ways: The use of renovated butter creates a market for the man who produces dairy butter and affords a cheap spread to those who desire to use it.
Do not imagine that I am trying to press this matter unduly; I want to give hon. members an opportunity to say what they think about it. Those who were in favour of a cheap spread being provided when we were discussing oleomargarine should hold up both hands for this measure. I am satisfied not only as to the quality of renovated butter, but as to its food content. I could read further on in this letter a statement about the vitamines that it contains, and if half the value attaches to vitamines that the scientists claim, that consideration is a very important one, especially when comparison is made with the other cheap spread that we have discussed.
I merely want to give an opportunity for an educative campaign by bringing this enactment into effect by proclamation. If the committee likes, I will incorporate in the bill a provision that the proclamation shall not issue for at least twelve months, so that the country may have an ppportunity of discussing it. The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) when Minister of Agriculture, brought down one of the best pieces of legislation introduced by the late government, namely, the Dairy Produce Act. That act was put into force by proclamation and the proclamation did not take place until nearly two years after the act was passed. That act met with a good deal of opposition from certain members. We are always fearful of changes in procedure which we have followed for forty years or so. It is not often I am in a position to speak in complimentary terms, not of the hon. member for Victoria City, but of the late government. I want to say to their credit, however, that they did put

this progressive legislation on the statute book, and we waited 'for two years before it was proclaimed law. During that time an educative campaign was carried on; the dairymen were finally ready to accept it, and you do not hear a murmur about it now. The system of grading butter and cheese as provided by that act simply glided into force, without leaving even a ripple on the surface. I am sure the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) will corroborate what I say as to the wisdom of that procedure. So it will be with this legislation; in
4 p.m. fact, the proclamation - will not issue at all if the people do not want it-I am sure I am not going to force it on them. But if they do want it after oleo goes out in March, I think it would be fair to give them the opportunity-that is all.

With regard to clause 2
of this resolution, I may point out that for a number of years the manufacture or importation into Canada of renovated butter has not been permitted. During those years Canada has made greater progress in her dairying than in any other period of her history. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in describing renovated butter. He said it was a product made from butter that contains too much salt, too much water, or too much curd-and he stopped there. The description would have been more accurate had he added, too much smell. He also said it was one hundred per cent butter fat, but he neglected to say it might be one hundred per cent rancid butter fat. If ordinary dairy butter does not have any of these objectionable features, there is no reason why it should not find a market in this country without any difficulty whatever. He speaks also about the pioneering that was done in the past, about our frontier farmers and about how we had to sell our dairy butter when there were no creameries. I remember those days very well indeed, but even then we had people who made butter of first-class quality in the dairies, and others who turned out a product that was as much butter as axle grease and commanded about the same price. I remember well the introduction of the creamery system, a step which put dairying on its feet in British Columbia. If in these outlying districts they cannot turn out a good quality of butter by the ordinary methods, then the next best thing is to encourage a co-operative creamery system. By doing that we can get away to a good start in the dairy business in these districts. A
Dairy Industry Act
good deal of objection can be urged against the introduction of this renovated butter. There is this about oleo: It is made from fresh ingredients, under the strictest possible inspection, with sanitary conditions prevailing in the abattoirs or packing houses in which it is manufactured that do not obtain in the average dairy. It is proposed by this resolution to permit a man to make any kind of dirty butter; to keep his cream separator as dirty as he likes-to wash it once or twice a week instead of twice a day; to milk his cows with dirty hands and as a result to get dirty cream; to keep the cream too warm; tc chum the butter badly, with the result that it is off in colour, in odour or in texture We propose to say to that man: Never mind; we are going to make you prosperous; we will provide a place where you can take your butter and have it deodorized so as to make it fit to eat. In my opinion it would be much better to begin with the farmer himself, to do what we can to teach him how to keep the cream; to impress upon him the necessity for cleanliness in his dairy; then, where there are three or four hundred cows in one locality, to encourage if possible the establishment of co-operative creameries. The dairyman should be taught right from the beginning that he cannot make a living out of the dairy business by milking a scrub cow and by producing a brand of butter that has to be deodorized at one of these factories before it can be sold. By following a system of that kind we can help to put the dairying of Canada on a much firmer basis than by any such proposal as is offered in clause 2 of this resolution.
Now, what is butter? According to United States law and the regulations governing its manufacture, butter is a food product made exclusively from milk or cream with or without salt or colouring matter. Renovated butter is described as butter which is subjected to any process by which it is melted, clarified or refined and made to resemble genuine butter. So you see the United States does not recognize renovated butter as genuine butter. In the United States large quantities of adulterated butter are manufactured; and I notice that the hon. minister has not referred to this in his resolution. The United States Government defines adulterated butter to mean a grade of butter produced by mixing, re-working, re-churning in milk or cream, refining or in any way producing a uniform, purified, or improved product from different lots or parcels of melted or unmelted butter or butter fat in which any acid, alkali, chemical, or any substance whatever is introduced or used for
Dairy Industry Act

the purpose or with the effect of deodorizing or removing therefrom rancidity; or any butter or butter fat with which there is mixed any substance foreign to butter as herein defined with intention or effect of cheapening in cost the product; or any butter in the manufacture or manipulation of which any process or material is used with intent or effect of causing the absorption of abnormal quantities of water, milk or cream. In the United States special taxes are applied to these products. On renovated butter there is a tax of a quarter of a cent per pound, and on adulterated butter a tax of ten cents per pound. Now, the general practice followed in renovating butter is to melt it at a temperature of fifty or sixty degrees. I wish to draw attention to this fact: That by melting at that low temperature you do not obtain any of the effects you might look for in properly pasteurized cream or milk, so that any germ contained in that butter may still remain. The water is separated from the oils that have been melted and then the impurities, the soluble impurities are washed out with clean water. Then it is aerated to remove the bad odors. After being laundered in this method it has neither taste, nor colour, nor odor, and to make it taste like butter it is necessary to restore its granular texture. This is done by spraying the liquid with ice cold water. Then butter colour is added to make it look like June butter. Finally the lactic sharp flavour which is so much in demand in good butter by adding a starter, or in other words lactic acid bacteria. Then the product is rolled out and worked in the ordinary way. It has been shown, though, that an oxidization takes place in this bleaching process. You will remember that in the oleo discussion it was brought out that the absence of vitamines was indicated very largely by the colour of butter; that the white winter butter was very low in vitamine content, while the June grass butter was highly yellow in colour indicating a richness of vitamines. So when this butter is washed out and bleached in this laundering process I have just described it has been lowered in vitamine content to a considerable extent. It therefore has not the same food value that ordinary butter would have. But, dressed up as it is in its new clothes, with a new smell, a new colour and so forth, it is quite suitable for fooling the public as far as butter buying is concerned. Then it has been shown not to be a good keeper. Professor Clayton, Master of Science, of Liverpool University, says:

Cleanliness is most essential at every stage during renovation and even then the keeping qualities of the product are much inferior to those of ordinarv butter.
Showing you how necessary it will be, if renovated butter is allowed to be produced in this country, to carefully guard against its being mixed with any product which we export to the Old Country.
In my opinion the legislation proposed is a retrograde step. As I pointed out a while ago the dairyman who has a cow perhaps that is giving 125 pounds of butter fat a year, is being jollied into the belief that he can continue *to make butter in a creamery in which his cream is carelessly kept, whilst his cow is housed in a dirty stable in winter, he is to be permitted to send the product down to the butter laundry where it will be deodorized and sold to the people. I do not think we should do anything of that kind. The sooner this man is informed that he cannot hope to carry on dairying successfully either with a scrub cow, or with such scrub methods on his dairy farm, the better it will be for him and for the dairy interests of Canada. In fact the government will be doing him a special favour to inform him on that point. There is nothing in this proposition for the farmer as far as I can see. The average dairy cow of Canada will yield from 125 to 150 pounds of butter fat in the year. Let us say, to give her the benefit of the doubt, she averaged 150 pounds and that her lactation period lasts 300 days. This would give her average as half a pound of butter fat per day. This bad butter, I understand, sells at from ten to thirteen cents a pound according to smell and appearance. We will give the benefit of the doubt again and allow twenty cents as the average for the year. That would be a return of just ten cents per day per cow for that farmer, and perhaps that butter needs deodorizing before it can be sold. Anyone will see that this is a hopeless proposition; it will benefit somebody. The man who operates that factory will buy this butter just as cheaply as he can, will put it through this renovating process, and then sell it at a fairly good price. It will also be a benefit to the butter speculator who will buy a certain quantity of butter when it is cheap, place it in cold storage, and then wait for a rise in the market. Quite frequently that butter goes off colour and goes off in condition, and if there is a renovating factory in the country he can always send the product down to the laundry, have it done over, and then serve it up again. This is decidedly unfair to the maker of good butter in Canada-to the man who keeps

a good herd of cattle, who is careful about his dairying methods, who observes cleanliness in the care of his separators, and milking utensils and milking operations. It is particularly unfair to the producer of butter in British Columbia where we have a fine creamery system established for a long time and which has rendered very excellent service to the dairy business. In addition to making butter of very excellent quality in British Columbia we are also importers; we bring in hundreds of tons of butter from outside points into that province to supply the wants of the people there. Therefore, if renovated butter is permitted then the British Columbia producer of good butter will have to compete with this much cheaper and inferior article. There is also a very great danger, as the minister has pointed out, of mixing this renovated butter with our export butter for the Old Country. I should just like to quote what has happened in the United States in this regard. I quote again from "The Butter Industry in the United States," page 157:
The amount of butter exported from this country has decreased considerably since 1890, when nearly 30 million pounds were exported. In 1914 the amount exported was less than 4 million pounds. This decline is due to several causes. With the appearance of oleomargarine and renovated butter large quantities of this stock were sent abroad marked as finest American creamery butter. This deception soon destroyed our reputation for making good butler, just as our reputation for making good cheese was lost by exporting adulterated and filled cheese.
Let me quote the Dairy and Food Commissioner of Michigan. In a report which deals with renovated butter he says:
One can scarcely conceive how the ill-made and spoilt country butter, after lying for weeks in the hot storeroom of the country merchants and becoming positively nauseating, can be worked over and made sufficiently deceiving as to be sold for creamery butter. The fact remains that that is done, and in Michigan, at least, tons of this worked-over renovated butter are sold for good butter with greater or less deceit.
Now, with regard to the mixing of oleo with butter, the test, for oleo is very similar to the test for this renovated or process butter, making it easy to find oleomargarine when it is added to creamery butter for the purpose of fraud, but being rather more difficult to discover whether any process or renovated butter has been added to the good article. Mixing this inferior butter with the good article which we propose to send over from Canada to Great Britain would have a tremendous effect on our British market, if we are going to get any hold on that market. With regard to the proposal to import this inferior butter from the United States, I think this is nothing short of outrageous. Why should we furnish a market in this country
for this outcast material from the country south of the line? We are about twenty years 'behind the times, too, in our move to introduce renovated butter into Canada. Let us see what has happened in the United States. In the year 1903, 54,658,790 pounds of renovated butter was made in the United States, and in the year 1921 this had decreased to 6,099,110, or a decrease of something over almost 90 per cent. In the meantime creamery butter has increased very considerably. To meet the situation of this man on the outskirts, who is situated in the newer provinces, distant from the market, my idea would be to instruct him as fully as possible, perhaps in co-operation with the provincial government, giving him full knowledge of the necessity of having the right kind of cow in his dairy and of dairying along the proper lines. This can be done through the Farmers' Institutes. It was done that way in British Columbia. I had to do with the organization of several creameries in that country, and I was working on institute work for the provincial government. If can be done through our printed matter, which is turned out by the Department of Agriculture in very large quantity every year, and it is very excellent matter. The encouragement of the establishment of co-operative creameries, the buying of the cream on grade, and then the full education of the farmer to the fact that if he wishes to succeed-and I stress this many times over-he must get the right kind of cow, and produce the turned-out products that will promise to him the largest possible price. Every one of us who has had any experience in the dairy business knows that we must get the highest price by producing the highest priced article, if we ever hope to succeed, which means that we must work 365 days each year. We should do everything possible to develop our export market, and I do not know what effect, with our butter, perhaps, falling back a little on the British market, it will have to advise the Britishers over there that we have now taken up the renovated butter making in Canada -something we never did before. I am sure it will not improve our position. I think we should turn out the best possible article, inspect the butter very very carefully, and add, as I have proposed "Canada approved," such as -we have attached to many of our agricultural products in this country, as an indication that we stand behind the goods. I think it is very regrettable that the hoa. minister has brought this important resolution before the House at this late date. We are very short of information.

If the provision of renovated butter for the poor man's spread is going to jeopardize the dairy industry to any extent, we will have to seek some other solution; because Canada will have to depend on its dairy industry as the cornerstone of agriculture.

"Adulterated butter" is hereby defined to mean a grade of butter produced by mixing, reworking, re-chuming in milk or cream, refining, or in any way producing a uniform, purified, or improved product from different lots or parcels of melted or unmelted butter or butter fat, in which any acid, alkali, chemical, or any substance whatever is introduced or used for the purpose or with the effect of deodorizing or removing therefrom rancidity, or any butter or butter fat with which there is mixed any substance foreign to butter as herein defined, with intent or effect of cheapening in cost the product, or any butter in the manufacture or manipulation of which any process or material is used with intent or effect of causing the absorption of abnormal quantities of water, milk or cream.
In the United States they treat rancid butter with an acid, alkali or chemical and make it into what is called adulterated butter. My hon. friend is going to take this rancid butter -which is picked up in our back yards, and which the dairy people refuse to market-and renovate it without treating it with any acid, alkali or chemical. Butter may be renovated and be without smell or taste, as the hon. minister said. But I say it is all taste and all odour, and will so remain notwithstanding its being designated as renovated butter.
If this butter is to be allowed to be brought into the Dominion, we are likely to have another industry. At present we have the rum bootlegger, and last year we had the cigarette bootlegger. Now we are going to have the renovated butter bootlegger, who will see to it that butter renovated or adulterated in the United States is brought in here without paying any tax. My hon. friend is being led astray by the fact that there is a loud ciy in Canada for a butter substitute. Renovated butter is not a butter substitute: it is a bad butter; it is a rancid butter; it is a rotten butter. If the minister can show the committee any means whereby he can renovate a butter without using an acid and thereby making it an adulterated butter, then he is a chemist for whom this country has been looking for some time.
I was just wondering where my hon. friend got his authority for what he says about using acids. Is there anything else in it except the lactic acid that is generated in milk or cream that is sour?
I am glad my hon. friend admits that degeneration takes place.
Not at all.

Why impose upon the people something that is degenerated? If from 1914 to 1918, when the people were considering the matter of substitutes for butter and other foods, they refused to have anything to do with renovated or adulterated butter, then I cannot understand why in a time of peace, when there is no cry for substitutes, we should go back to a period that we have long since outlived. My hon. friend talks about a spread. Is he aware that the official spread for bread to-day in the British navy is oleomargarine? The British navy is developing the best athletes in the world. I do not say they are doing it on oleomargarine, but I do say that the physicians of the English navy, who are noted for their judgment and fair-mindedness, have approved of a regulation making oleomargarine the official spread for the navy's bread.
We are not talking about oleomargarine now; we are debating the question of butter.

Well, I am talking about both. But I shall not disturb the dreams of my hon. friend very much longer. I am not a dairyman; I have not a cow and perhaps never will have one, but I have some interest in the people of this country. A week ago the minister stood in his place and opposed the manufacture and importation of a product which is recognized in the British navy as a substitute for butter. He now tells the committee that it is necessary for the poor man of this country that the manufacture and importation of renovated butter be permitted. I do suggest that in view of all the circumstances he should give the matter a little more serious consideration than he has given it.

I have been listening very
attentively to the discussion, but I have not got complete light on the situation yet. It has been stated that it is more difficult to detect renovated butter when mixed with ordinary butter than it is to detect oleomargarine when used in the same way. If that is the case, it will be difficult to prevent fraud.
What means will be adopted as a
5 p.m. protection against fraud or misrepresentation? Furthermore, in regard to the chemical changes which may be produced in butter through its being kept for long periods at a fairly high temperature, how far is it possible to remove the various products of decomposition which result from these changes? It may be fairly easy to deodorize the product to a certain extent by aeration, but it strikes me it is a very

Dairy Industry Act

much more difficult process effectively to remove the products of decomposition. Then, I should like to know something about the question of sterilizing. It has been maintained that butter used in the manufacture of renovated butter would be not so good on the average as creamery butter. Of course, a good deal of the butter manufactured under primitive conditions is perfectly clean, or at least as clean as the average creamery butter. But I am inclined to think that the butter that will find its way into the renovating factories will be a product which has been manufactured by careless people under conditions which may bring about contamination. I do not think there is anything in the renovating process which is designed to afford protection against disease germs, and I would like to have some information on that point. It does seem to me that the minister is adopting a very extraordinary attitude after his vote the other day on the oleomargarine question.

I beg my hon.
friend's pardon; I did not speak on it the other day.

I was not referring to the
minister's Speaking on it; I was referring to his voting on the question. It is not necessary on all occasions to speak to a subject in order to indicate one's attitude. I have always been of the opinion that, under proper regulation and supervision to guard against fraud and misrepresentation, oleomargarine is a perfectly suitable food product, and I sincerely hope that before the end of the present session, perhaps in connection with this bill, the House will have a chance to declare itself on this particular issue, wholly apart from the issues that entered into the discussion and the vote the other day. The minister talks about the poor man's spread. It is necessary for us to have some regard to that phase of the question, but it seems to me that this renovated butter is likely to be a poorer, a more dangerous poor man's spread than oleomargarine. I have no objections to renovated butter; in that respect I hold the same view as I do in regard to oleomargarine. I do not object to it provided that we can certify as to its quality, as to its wholesomeness, and provided also that we can protect the public against fraud and misrepresentation. Until we get more information on these points it seems to me that we are, to quote the old saying, "straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel." I hope the minister can give the committee some further infor-marirn on these questions Let me repeat

them again, because I think the minister was not paying attention when I started to speak.
I think I heard the questions.
There is the question of misrepresentation, the question of removing the products of decomposition, and the question of sterilization.

I think the hon. gentleman's attitude is quite reasonable. But the resolution provides exactly what he asked for. We are not going into this matter in such a tremendous hurry. The hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll) seemed to think that to-morrow or the day after the bill became law, we would be shouting renovated butter round the streets. That is not so. Here is my proposal: If the House sends this bill to the select standing committee on Agriculture my intention is to follow the same course that we have adopted in the case of three or four other bills, bring the experts of the Department of Agriculture before the committee to give evidence on the very things my hon. friend speaks about. What else can you do? You cannot bring these experts before the House. Furthermore, I am prepared to suggest now that the word "importation" be struck out from the bill. I will discuss the matter with the proper authorities and see if that can be done without doing violence to our international relations, or being accused of anything that would look like unfriendliness towards other nations. I do not like to see that word "importation" used. I will be quite frank with the House and say that the experts in the Dairy branch differ on this question. Some of	them do	not	like it.After this has	been	prohibited for	twentyyears they do	not	like the	idea	of reintroducing it.	Others take	the	ground
that it never should have been prohibited, that it should have been permitted all along. We will submit evidence to the committee from experts, and to the extent the witnesses seem to favour a departure in the matter we will give the industry the benefit of the doubt. But let us try to get to the bottom of the matter.

Does the minister propose to
submit this bill to the committee on Agriculture after its second reading?

When reference of a bill to a committee is proposed it is always done after a second reading. Any section of this bill could be eliminated in the Agriculture committee without destroying any principle embodied in it. As a matter of fact, the bill

to amend the Live Stock Act was so completely changed in committee that we had to reprint it.
When will the bill be submitted to the committee?

Just as soon as possible. I understand we are going to have morning sittings next week so that we would have to do it on Monday.
Now, just let me run over two or three matters that have been raised during the discussion. Certain members have described the product we are dealing with. It was stated by the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) that this renovated butter is so good that it is sent over to the United Kingdom from the United States and passes there for creamery butter.
An hon. "MEMBER: It is mixed with other butter.
Well, it is mixed if you like. But even so, it cannot be as bad as it has been described; you cannot fool people that way.

The minister is hardly giving to what I said the interpretation I intended. What I tried to point out was that there had been so much fraudulent shipping of oleomargarine and renovated butter to Great Britain that it had caused a serious falling off in the export of American butter to that country.

But we cannot have the product so good that it is taken for creamery butter, and at the same time so bad that the smell of it is enough to knock you down. I have promised to have this bill referred to the committee on Agriculture. I believe there is a question involved that is worth looking into, and worth solving, for the purpose of meeting the dairyman's views on the one hand and the views of the man who wants cheap butter on the other. If we can do that we shall be performing a good service. Let the bill go to the committee on Agriculture, and if they feel that any section is wrong or is unwise it can be eliminated. There is nothing mysterious about that. We. removed three or four sections from the bill to amend the Live Stock Act. I should like to see the word "importation" struck out and I will move that that be done now. I do not like the thought of importation, but I am not a bit afraid myself of any importation taking place. I think it is only an imaginary difficulty, something that will never arise. But even imaginary difficulties sometimes hurt more than difficulties that are real.

This resolution and the
matter it deals with are very important. It will not do for the minister to answer a civil question put to him across the floor by a somewhat crude intimation that the questioner is ignorant of the subject he is talking about. I must say that outside of the Minister of Agriculture I think I can compliment most of the members of the government, when in committee of the whole, with at least behaving with attentive courtesy and giving civil answers to those who question them in a polite and proper manner.
That is terrible.

The Minister of Agriculture seldom presents anything to the House which calls for debate without making more or less of a burlesque of the whole proceedings. He has not abandoned or departed from his record in that respect this afternoon. I therefore think it would be better for me to address what observations I have to make more to the Prime Minister than to the Minister of Agriculture.

That is politeness
itself.

My remarks have greatly to do with the propriety and desirability of advancing this legislation at this late period in the, session. May I point out to the Prime Minister this: In the first place there is decided opposition to this legislation in the country. I have in my hand a telegram from the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association. This association consists of 1,800 farmers in the Fraser valley who have banded themselves together for the marketing of their products, that is milk, butter and other products. It markets its products direct to the consumer, and perhaps is one of the best and most highly organized co-operative associations in existence in Canada. The telegram reads as follows:	*
We understand that resolution is being introduced in parliament permitting the importation, manufacture and sale of renovated butter. We strongly protest against the government granting such permission. Same will be very detrimental to the dairy interests of this country.
I submit this to the Prime Minister. I have already submitted it to the Minister of Agriculture and I think it would perhaps add to the burlesquing of this matter if I read the minister's letter to the House.
Will my hon. friend read his own letter as well?

Yes, if it is desirable.

If my answer is
read I should like my hon. friend to read his letter to me.
I will read them both.
Sure.

I have received another
telegram from George Sangster, on behalf of the Vancouver Island Milk Producers' Association, incorporated in which are, perhaps, the main dairymen and producers of Vancouver Island. The telegram reads as follows:
Milk producers of Vancouver Island absolutely opposed to resolution to permit importation, manufacture and sale of renovated butter. Please use every effort to defeat this measure as we consider it would impose unfair and impossible competition and deal a death blow to the dairy industry.
Here are two large associations-and I submit this to the Prime Minister in particular- I suppose numbering upwards of 3,000 members, of dairymen, with mostly large herds, 20, 30, 40, or 50 head of cattle, all marketing their products directly to the people, and both these associations declaring that this measure is very very detrimental. On this request I base my argument. This product has been barred from the Canadian market for 20 years. Why, within one week of the end of the session, introduce legislation to permit the manufacture of this product in Canada-I shall deal with the proclamation feature later -without giving opportunity to such interests as these to whom I have referred-and doubtless there are other interests in other parts of Canada-a fair opportunity to be heard before the committee on Agriculture? It will be at once recognized by this committee that there is no possibility whatever of the dairy interests of Canada being heard next Monday morning. That is an absurdity. It is only an evidence of the insincerity of the minister and the deliberate desire on his part to rush this measure through, not only without due consideration, but without a remnant of fairness to the industries so vitally interested.
Did these two large dairying interests in British Columbia not make similar representations against oleo, which the hon. member ignored?

Not to me. I am merely reading what I have received. I admit, with reference to the mild indictment of my hon. friend that, perhaps, I am not as well posted, or as well qualified, to speak on this question, as some hon. members. I see across the way my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Munro) who, I know, is well qualified to speak. He represents one of the best dairying districts in Canada, but, on the other hand, let

me say to the minister that I am not altogether void of knowledge of the dairy business. I spent a great many years in my early days on an Ontario farm, and I have been interested in western farming for the last ten years. I do not parade that fact, because I think it is inadvisable for one who is not actually and definitely a farmer to emphasize the fact that he knows something about farming. I used that fact as a retort that I am not wholly ignorant of the subject. The minister challenged me to read my letter to him and his letter to me. I will do so. My letter to him is dated June 18, and reads:
Ottawa, June 18th, 1923.
Hon. W. R. Motherwell,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Motherwell,
I enclose herewith two telegrams from the Vancouver Independent Milk Producers' Association and the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association, Vancouver, objecting to your bill to provide for the manufacture and sale of "renovated" butter.
I beg to advise you that it is my intention when this matter comes before the House, to urge for the withdrawal of this bill for this session and suggest the submission of the whole subject to the Agricultural committee next year. I see no reason for haste in the passing of such legislation and, furthermore, I most respectfully submit that your action in promoting this bill is wholly inconsistent with the attitude you took, as Minister of Agriculture, in recently opposing the manufacture and sale of a perfectly wholesome food, namely, oleomargarine.
You undoubtedly know that in the process of manufacturing so called renovated butter deleterious chemicals are used and I am amazed that you, as Minister of Agriculture, would be so indifferent to the creamery and dairy interests of this country as to introduce such a bill.
I therefore earnestly suggest that you withdraw this bill for this session and refer the whole question to the Agricultural committee next session.
Yours very sincerely,
H. H. Stevens.
That is the letter I wrote to the minister. His reply is dated June 19th, and reads:
Ottawa, 19th June, 1923.
The Honourable H. H. Stevens, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Stevens,
Your favour of the 18th instant just received.
Replying I have to thank you for your quite decided views regarding renovated butter. I may say that I have myself been endeavouring for a number of years to estimate the value of this product as a cheaper spread than creamery butter for those who do not feel they are warranted in paying the higher price.
Last year when the oleo. discussion was up I promised the House that, in the event of oleo. being prohibited. I would advise my colleagues to make legislative provision to remove the prohibition of the manufacture of renovated butter, on the ground that the fat of the latter consists of 100 per cent butter fat, contains all the essential vitamines and growth properties, and consequently would seem to be a more logical, cheap spread than ordinary gut fat, which has usually been used as soap grease in times past and even yet. However, even in a matter so obvious as this, experts seem to differ.

It is my intention to have this question discussed before the Agricultural committee-not next year but this year, when a number of authorities can be asked to give evidence in the same manner as I have done with my other bills this session.
I think you are a member of the Agricultural committee and I should be very pleased to have the benefit of your advice and suggestions when the matter is then under discussion. I might point out also that the provision with respect to renovated butter is merely one section of a bill, the balance of which, I feel confident, will meet with your entire approval. Your suggestion, therefore, that the bill be withdrawn will, I think, be opposed by yourself when you understand all the circumstances.

There is nothing in that of any importance, but I read it because my hon. friend desires to have it read.
Let me turn to one or two other phases of the matter. My hon. friend says he mentioned this a year ago. Now he says that one of these resolutions provides that the legislation will be ineffective for a year at least. He will promise the House that the proclamation will not be made until after next March. This is what I want the committee to consider: After mentioning this over a year ago why did the minister not introduce it early in the session and let the committee deal with it while the sittings of this House were proceeding? t If, on the other hand, it was not desirable to introduce it early this year, so the committee could study it, and it is not his intention to bring the legislation into effect until after next March, why not let it stand over till next year and give the committee of Agriculture an opportunity to discuss it properly, and give the interests affected an opportuninty to appear before the committee? In order to take that stand, it is not necessary for me to be opposed to the matter on principle at all. I am merely dealing with the desirability of forcing matter through during the last days of the session. Surely, nothing will be lost by postponing this for a year, when for over twenty years there has been no such commodity produced in Canada. Who is to be hurt? The minister himself says, "If there is no demand for it"-I have his words here, because I always find it necessary to write them down, if I wish to put a question in regard to them-"the proclamation will not be made; if there is a demand we will issue the proclamation." Why not wait and delay the legislation, to see if there is a demand? Why not wait to give those affected an opportunity to express their views pro or con?
There is another matter I wish to refer to. Most able reference has been made by
my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) who speaks on all such subjects with authority, and not only with authority, but with ability, and in a manner becoming the dignity of the House. He referred to the fact that the whole effort of the agricultural departments of the provinces and the Dominion in connection with the pure foods administration of the country has been pressing towards making a highclass product, and obtaining better methods of dairying and creamery butter production, and he pointed out that one of the effects of encouraging the use of renovated butter was to encourage the reproduction of inferior or carelessly made butter. The minister said that butter would deteriorate. He said "It will get rotten and does get rotten." He also said, "If you expose eggs to the weather, to the sun and the warm temperature, will they not get rotten?" But is the minister proposing next session to bring in a measure for renovated eggs-to make rotten eggs marketable? That is the next thing we shall hear about, from the Minister of Agriculture. As I listened to the minister this afternoon going through that effort to ridicule the splendid and scientific presentation of this question by the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), I thought his indictment of the dairy industry of this country was one of the most damning that I had ever heard. If anyone took seriously the utterances of the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, that the butter products of this country were produced as he intimated they were, that the slaughtering of animals and the extraction of the various parts were carried out in the manner he described, that would be one of the most injurious things to the dairying industry anil the butter production industry of Canada.
What has the slaughtering of animals to do with the dairy industry?
I wondered myself when my hon. friend pictured, in a somewhat disgusting fashion, the puncturing of the intestines of an animal.
I would suggest that til's argument is getting a little rotten.
I was not talking about butter then.

The presentation by the minister of the case from his standpoint this afternoon was not in the interest of the promotion of the production of butter this country.

Is the president or the manager of this Fraser Valley Milk Association the same person who, when the question of reducing the price of milk in Vancouver was up, said: "To hell with the public"?

I do not remember the incident mentioned by my hon. friend, nor do I know. I do not quite see the pertinence of the question. All I know is this-and I know this from personal acquaintance wi 1>
many of them-that the Fraser Valley Milk Producers' Association is what I said it was, namely a combination of some 1,800 farmers, dairymen, producing milk, marketing it directly to the people of Vancouver, New Westminster and other centres, and manufacturing very large quantities of butter. Outside of that I know nothing more of what the president may have said in a fit of temper or may not. have said.
While the minister may accuse me of ignorance of some matters which may seem to be very familiar to him, I, at least, as a public man, or as a private citizen, ought to have some interest in the promotion of the dairying business and the foreign trade of Canada. One of the things we have been striving as a nation to do for the last twenty years is to raise the general standard of our products, to bring these products to such a uniformity of standard that they will earn a place on the British or European market in competition with the highly developed dairy industry of Denmark. In the very interesting booklets sent to me day after day by the minister-and if the minister issues these booklets, surely he expects us to read them -I was reading an indictment of the Canadian dairy industry to a certain extent on the very point that they were not keeping up the standard of uniformity of butter in Canada m competition with Denmark. Within a week they showed us figures that the Denmark exportation to the British market had increased enormously, while the Canadian exportation had decreased. That is something in wh'ch I am interested, and I do not intend to be silenced by the rebuff from the minister that I am supposed to know nothing about the subject. I am not speaking dogmatically, but many feel that the introduction of this resolution as regards the production of renovated butter in Canada on a large scale, will tend to lower the general standard cf Canadian butter produced for export. Let me tell the committee why. We know perfectly well that renovated butter is deodorized; the objectionable visible features, shall I say, are taken out of it, that is the question of odour and the question of bad taste, by 
certain chemical processes. It is washed in lime or lime materials and other things, and these are eliminated. When it is manufactured, as I am told by those who know and who are in a position to advise, there is, perhaps, difficulty at a glance to tell the difference between it and fairly good creamery butter, but the minute the inspector sees it, he discovers it. Take a shipment of say 60,000 cases of butter going on the London or Liverpool market, or wherever it may go. They test every one in 10 or 20, as the case may be, according to the usual method of test. It might be possible to slip into such a shipment quite a large number of cases of butter not up to standard. That has been one of the complaints against Canadian butter, that running through our Canadian butter there are at times inferior cases. What I wish to impress upon the minister, and particularly on the Prime Minister at this time, is that many of us think the introduction of this legislation will tend to vitiate the policy followed by this government and previous governments, namely of raising the standard of general dairy products. We do not wish that to be brought about. I am not saying it will, but at least let us have a reasonable time to study the question.
Does my hon. friend know whether the renovation prevails in any country except the United States?

I am not in a position to answer that question. I would not answer it because I cannot answer it correctly and definitely. Let me say this, in conclusion: It will be utterly impossible to give a fair hearing to this matter this session before the Agricultural committee. We begin sitting in the morning next week, and we hope to get through by the end of next week. These interests, therefore, cannot be heard. I have made certain representations, very weak, on their behalf; but they and other interests cannot be heard. The minister says that he does not intend to bring this proclamation in for a year. Then why pass the legislation? Why fix upon the country a definite statutory law, when you acknowledge that you have not had time for consideration, and when it is clear that these interests cannot be heard. So I ask the Prime Minister most earnestly that this measure, as regards renovated butter, should be allowed to stand over until next year, and that all interests should be heard before the Agriculture committee. Personally I shall be glad to abide by the decision of that committee, after a reasonable and fair hearing of the subject.
