speechtext: The minister has intimated clearly that his intention is to refer the bill to the Agriculture committee. That committee is, perhaps, in a better position than the House to decide whether it would be wise to have this particular clause stand over for another year. If the committee has the slightest doubt as to the wisdom of proceeding with that clause, the government would be only too happy to accept the finding of the committee on that point. It will, perhaps, facilitate matters, seeing that we are discussing the resolution merely at the moment, if the committee were to pass the resolution and let the bill go to the Agriculture committee, with the understanding that if that committee is in the slightest doubt about the wisdom of proceeding with that particular question, the government will not press that part of the bill. Moreover, coupled with that, the members may take into account the minister's assurance that he will see that the proclamation under which this would become law, will be, at least, one year's time distant from the present, and this would give the opportunity of another session of parliament to consider the matter if it were thought advisable to do so.

That is really my strongest point. I wish the Prime Minister would consider it again after we pass from this stage. If you are going to consider the question in the interim between the assumed passing of the measure and the proclamation, would not it be better to consider the matter before the legislation is passed?

I have had the misfortune once or twice of treading on the toes of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). That hon. gentleman does not like my style of debate. I am sorry for that; but I seem to get along very well with it, and as it is the only kind of style I have I am afraid my hon. friend will have to put up with it, however distasteful it may be to him. He calls that style a burlesque, and strange to say he appears to think that I should accept that description with good grace. I was not very long in the House, as a matter of fact, before the hon. gentleman began to apply such descriptive phrases to myself, as "the Minister of Agriculture's burlesque." And when I modestly suggest that he does not know anything at all about dairying, why, he gets mad. I do not see why he should take umbrage at a statement so obviously true. Now, we cannot expect to give without occasionally being asked to take, in return; and surely, as a sportsman, my hon. friend should be ready to take what is coming to him, especially when it is so richly deserved as on this occasion.
Just one word or two, however. The hon. gentleman says that I have not given a civil answer. I replied to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) in the only way that I could possibly have replied to him. Sometimes such strange things are said that one can answer them only by ridicule, which, by the way, is very often the most effective method. An attempt is made at a description of chemicals. Is lactic acid a chemical? What do we usually mean when we talk of chemicals? Surely no one will describe as decomposition the natural process that takes place in the course of the manufacture of many e&cellent articles of diet such as bread, for example. Is there any decomposition in the manufacture of silage, or of any of those things in which certain necessary bacterial action takes place? If the decomposition which takes place in the manufacture of these things were the harmful process which hon. gentlemen seem to suggest, then some of the finest products we have would be noxious. So that when hon. gentlemen talk about "decomposition" in the way they do they only display a lack of knowledge of which it surely is no harm to remind them. If I delved into any question involving legal technicalities hon. gentlemen would most undoubtedly be justified if they reminded me that I was discussing a subject with which I was not particularly conversant.
I did not say that the putrefaction that took place was not due to bacterial action. There are four or five kinds of bacteria responsible for the changes that occur in the process of decomposition.

I was replying in this instance to my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). Now, I am not trying to force this thing through, and I do not think that I have appeared to be particularly wedded to the question. I have as open a mind in regard to the matter as anyone in the committee, and I recognize that it would take a great deal of explanation to show why, after a prohibition of twenty years, the manufacture of this product should be permitted. It would be much easier for me not to introduce the subject if I wanted to take the course of least resistance. If the committee will accept the Prime Minister's suggestion, of referring the matter to the committee on Agriculture, I promise to use no more influence than my unassisted vote, if it does come to a vote, to put it through. And if there is any doubt on the part of the committee as to the wisdom of the action we propose, we will defer the question not for a day or a month only, but, so far as I am concerned at any rate,
Dairy Industry Act

forever. We do not want to jeopardize in the least degree the dairying industry of the country, but we do want to take care of a situation that may arise when butter suddenly runs up in price beyond the reach of poor people. If the suggestion of the Prime Minister is acceptable to the committee we will eliminate this section. There is no need for any heated controversy over the section. We will drop it and go on with the rest of the measure in the usual way.

One serious objection to the procedure proposed by the minister is that Monday forenoon is apparently the only time the committee will have for the consideration of the matter, which is one of much importance. Moreover, the attendance in the com-mitte on Monday will in all probability be very small, owing to the fact that the election takes place in Ontario on that day. It seems to me that the wise policy would be to defer the whole matter for a year, so far at least as this particular clause is concerned, so that we may go into the particulars of it more fully in the meantime.

I realize the situation that will exist on Monday, but inasmuch as the House will not meet next week until eleven o'clock there is no reason why the Agriculture committee could not meet at ten o'clock so that we might have a full hour for as many days as might be necessary to discuss the subject. Indeed, I do not think it would take many days to dispose of the question after the committee had heard the evidence of the experts.
There will be practically no members from Ontario present on Monday.
I am speaking of Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday.

I do not wish to let the occasion pass without joining in the protest, not only against the principle of this legislation, but more particularly against the decision of the government to introduce it at this time. All hon. members are aware that many of the representatives from the dairy districts in Ontario are at this moment engaged in other matters than agriculture, and we have not their advice on this important question. It is very apparent that few people who are really interested in this legislation have had an opportunity of presenting their case to the minister, and certainly they will have no opportunity of appearing before the committee. The Prime Minister has suggested that when the matter is before the 
committee the government will not press this particular part of the bill. The minister himself has stated that he has an open mind with reference to the matter and is not particularly biassed one way or the other. At least, I regard that as his attitude. This legislation has been waiting 20 years now, and parliament has been sitting for the past six months. Yet the government desires to press this matter through in six days. On what ground are^ they justified in endeavouring to lailroad this legislation through parliament in so short a space of time? The minister himself has told us that if there is any doubt in the matter he is prepared to defer it not only for a day or a month, but forever. In other words, he expresses the willingness on the part of the government to do the fair thing by everyone interested and give the matter proper consideration. Under these circumstances, is there any reason why the whole subject, without being referred to any committee, cannot be allowed to stand over until next session in order that full justice may be done all persons interested? Large institutions like the Fraser Valiev Milk Producers' Association are vitally interested in this matter; and this particular organization, comprising some 1,800 members, have sent me a telegram stating their point of view. The wholesale producers who deal in this product as well as the consuming public, as represented in various organizations, will also undoubtedly desire to declare their position in the matter. For my part therefore I cannot see any reason why the minister or the government should object to the reasonable request of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), which if voted on would, I am sure, be supported by the majority of the committee.

Since this subject has been on the order paper we have had no protests against the legislation apart from the telegrams that have come from British Columbia, where I am sure the people are not acquainted with the real facts of the case. From among all the members of the National Dairy Council I have not had one protest against it. However, with a view to getting into touch with some of those who are interested in the subject, I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

Section 2 provides:
That no person shall manufacture pure shorts and shorts and mill screenings at the same mill.
It occurs to me that if this were put into force every mill in Canada would have to go out of business.

It is rather interesting
to hear the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb). I was anxious to learn his views on the resolution. As far as I know, there should not be very great objection to the main idea behind this proposed legislation, but I do not want to appear to commit myself and others here to the principle in detail when we come to the bill, because I see there is some difference between the bill and the resolution, the details being more clearly set forth in the former.

I think it might
be well to explain how these amendments came to be proposed. As the committee are aware, the adulterating of mill by-products with screenings has been authorized by law during the last few years. A number of complaints have been made to the department, particularly by farmers, as to the bad effect that some of these mill feeds containing screenings has on young pigs, the deaths of a number of animals being attributed to such feeds. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) brought the matter to my attention some time ago, and I promised to bring down legislation to deal with the trouble. Before doing so I thought it well
to consult the advisory board which the Seed Control Act provides for. This board represents the milling, live stock, dealers and other interests concerned. It met in this city and this bill is the result of their cogitations. The very section the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) calls attention to is a compromise. Mr. Cornell, secretary of the National Millers' Association, and Mr. Watts, secretary of the Dominion Millers' Association, were present, and they, on behalf of the milling interests, accepted this as a compromise. Middlings have to be sold in their purity because this is the only article that can be fed to young pigs, there being too much fibre in bran for them to assimilate. The millers take the ground that inasmuch as we compel them to sell middlings and bran in a pure state they should be allowed to make some disposition of the screenings the farmers sell with the wheat. They suggest that they be permitted to mix shorts with screenings as a feed for dairy cattle, to whom it would not be deleterious. Shorts is simply fine bran.

The millers pay nothing for
the screenings, which really belong to the farmer, being treated as dockage. What right, therefore, have the millers to mix these screenings and sell them as cattle feed?

I am not pleading
that the millers have any right to do so. I am simply pointing out that several interests are involved in this matter and that after discussing it for two or three days this resolution was the compromise they reached. I appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend, but the fact remains that screenings do get into wheat to a certain extent and are paid for as wheat.

Were the western millers
represented in the conference?

Mr. Watts and
Mr. Cornell between them represented the organized millers of Canada. I expected that the question would be raised, because there was a feeling of resentment against mixing these products at all. Inasmuch as a certain amount of dairy feed is required, it is suggested that screenings should be mixed with shorts for the purpose. I should like to have the views of the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) and the hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy), both of whom I understand have had a good deal of experience in dairying. There was a three day discussion on this somewhat involved question-the advisory board is there for this very purpose-and it does seem to be a fair compromise. It is
Feeding Stuffs Act

now provided that you cannot put any of these things into this mill stuff, even after you have bought it from the farmers and paid for it.

I would like to commend the minister for the main principle involved in this resolution. When the Feeding Stuffs bill was introduced in 1920 I took occasion to suggest to the then Minister of Agriculture that he provide in his bill that bran, pure shorts, middlings and those feeds that are generally looked upon as standard feeds be sold in their pure state. The bill which was passed at that time contemplated the mixing of screenings and other things with those feeds. I was glad to see the minister bring down a measure for the purpose of ensuring that these feeds particularly should be sold in their pure state, but I am a little sorry to see him weakening to the extent of suggesting that he does not care about the rest so long as middlings are sold in their pure state. That principle is just as important in its application to bran and shorts as it is in its application to middlings.

Does my hon. friend think it makes the shorts a less desirable dairy feed if the screenings are ground and mixed with it? I am not too sure about that myself. If they are good screenings, the result is an excellent feed, but I admit that it depends on the nature of the screenings. Shorts is only fine bran; there is very little middlings in it.

The mixing of screenings with shorts or bran or any of the feeds specified in this resolution will certainly lower their feeding value. If a miller wishes to compound a feed or to make a feed out of the screenings he takes out of the wheat, why should he not, if it has any feeding value, sell it on its own merits, having the contents set forth on a tag as specified in the regulations applying to all feeds? If there is any feeding value in his product he can do that and sell it at a lower price, but he should not be allowed to mix screenings which are of low feeding yalue-some are and some are not-with these feeds. I suggest that the minister carry out the main principle of his resolution.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I promised my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) that we would take up the matter to which he referred this afternoon as soon as the private bills were disposed of. I understand it will be nine o'clock before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will be able to take his seat, and if my hon. friend from Brandon will allow that matter to stand till that time we will take it up then.
All right.
House again in committee on the resolution of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to provide for the amendment of the Feeding Stuffs Act, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

It seems to me that the point raised before six o'clock is worth a little

Feeding Stuffs Act
further discussion, as to whether or not the miller should be permitted to incorporate any of the ground screenings in the mill offal.
I do not think this matter has received very much attentionTand I think it should receive further attention before the resolution is adopted.

I may say that
after six o'clock I took advantage of the opportunity of discussing this matter with a number of members opposite, including the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) who is not in his seat and I understand will not be in the House this evening. I have the suggestion made by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb), and the intimation that he did not think the resolution as drafted practicable with respe't to the mixing of screenings with shorts, especially under subclause 2 which says:
That no person shall manufacture pure shorts and shorts and mill screenings at the same mill.
That provision he thinks, as a practical miller, is impracticable, and I am disposed to give some heed to an authority of that nature, especially when it is accompanied by such a practical suggestion as that made by the' hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy), who suggests that all the by-products of the mill should be manufactured in their purity and sold in their purity. That is to say, we would have pure bran, pure shorts, pure middlings, and pure low grade flour. This is my suggestion: Inasmuch as the screenings are bought and paid for as wheat, millers should be permitted, in grinding those screenings, to mix with them any of those by-products that they may think are necessary in order to make those screenings acceptable to the market as long as they call the product screenings. In other words, these mill screenings, let us say, are ground and mixed with a portion of either bran or shorts or middlings, if the millers so desire. They will not mix middlings, because that is too expensive, but they may find it convenient to mix some shorts with the screenings. So long as they sell that as mill screenings, I can see no objection, particularly in view of the fact that they have bought and paid for the whole gross product as wheat. That is the alternative proposition. Because of its simplicity and the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the present draft, with the exception of the first section, is not practicable, I should like to have the other suggestion of the hon. member for Glengarry discussed by the committee. If that is acceptable to the committee as a
practical solution after it has been discussed,
I am disposed to accept it.

I am pleased that the minister is inclined to accept the logical suggestion made by the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy), and I hope concurred in by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think this is the logical conclusion. There should be no objection to selling mill screenings if there is any feed value in them, but they should not be camouflaged as shorts or anything else. If the millers see fit to mix bran or shorts in the screenings to make the mixture more palatable and of a better feed value, I can see no objection to that, so long as it is sold as screenings; but I do object to screenings being sold as shorts, or as a mixture of shorts and screenings, because, though it is provided in the bill that they should use only the run of mill screenings in the shorts, that is the screenings taken from the wheat from which the shorts are made, I see a difficulty in carrying out the regulation. It would be almost impossible to carry it out, and I think the minister's suggestion is the logical solution of the situation.

Before the House rose, I asked the minister a question concerning this. I might state that on all occasions when bills of this nature have come up, since I have had the honour of being in this House, I have protested against the conduct of millers in the past when they have mixed buckwheat, wild oats, and so forth, in bran, and have sold that as bran. I have been charged as high as S30 a ton for supposed bran which contained a large proportion of wild oats for which they paid nothing. It is a fact that milling companies in western Canada have their initial points throughout the country, and invariably their elevators are constructed without cleaning machinery. As a result of that, they gather in wild oats and buckwheat, which is prevalent and current in the West. They deduct the weight of this largely by guess, and no remuneration for this at all is offered to the individual, although they, in selling back feed stuffs put this value on it. I have protested against milling companies being allowed to use wild oats and even pigweed, and then returning the product to us as bran, shorts and various mill feeds, although they paid nothing for these things. As the minister explained this afternoon, these have a deleterious effect on young stock. With the provision that bran shall be sold as bran, and shorts as shorts, and the other by-products
Feeding Stuffs Act

similarly, possibly a provision might be incorporated that, as pigweed has not much milling value, it might be mentioned in the bill that pigweed could be screened out and whatever there might be in the way of other oats, tame oats, flax, wild buckweat, would make a very good commercial feeding stock to be sent back and sold as such. I commend the action of the minister in segregating the bran and shorts and things of that nature. I might protest that under the Grain Act milling companies at initial points, might be obliged to pay somewhat more for these foreign seeds found in grain, because milling companies which have gathering points on the prairies have an advantage over straight grain companies, in that not having cleaning facilities at their elevators throughout the West, they do not pay for these things.

Is it correct
that wild oats are sown on the prairies?

Wild oats have not been
particularly sown. Persons who sow wild oats do not boast of how many bushels they reap per acre. Some wild oats may make fair feed, but not for young calves.

I would go further than the
suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture. I would have not only the bran and shorts pure, but the screenings pure. There is no necessity to allow people who are selling screenings to mix shorts or anything else with them, even though they are going to be compelled to call that screenings. I know how soon an arrangement of that kind can enlarge itself, so to speak, and pretty soon there would be a great deal of shorts in it, and it would be called by some composite name, more or less calculated to deceive people. Let us have these things pure. Let those who want to buy or who have that class of stock that can eat screenings mixed with something else, buy it themselves and mix it themselves. Then the}^ will know what they are doing, and there will be no possibility of adulteration or fraud, or even of renovating. It is just as illogical to mix shorts and screenings, as, I dare say, to mix oleomargarine with butter and then sell it as butter.

My hon. friend
thinks that will appeal to me.

I should like to suggest that the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Albcrni (Mr Neill) should be given serious attention. I can very easily see how the opening might be used for the gradual ad-

mixture of various products with the screenings, disguising them and probably defeating the very object we have in view. It seems to me that the legislation contemplated is, in the main, admirable. It is something that has been needed for a long time, and I should like to endorse it very much. The minister, however, might go just a little further and make it necessary for those who wish to feed screenings, to do their own mixing, and not to have the mixing done at the point of manufacture. I might mention, too, in that connection, that I think it is very necessary to have these screenings tagged-probably that is compulsory anyway-with tags stating the composition of the feed. I should like to know also whether or not provision is made for the elimination of unpalatable and poisonous weeds from these screenings. Is there any law applying to that?

The argument of
the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) seems quite logical on the surface, but when one remembers that these screenings are bought and paid for as wheat it would seem to partake of the nature of poetic justice that the millers should be allowed when grinding the screenings to mix with them a proportion of shorts in order to produce a better compound for the market. I am not an advocate of the millers, but I certainly do not think that we should go so far in our restrictions as to hurt unreasonably not only them but ourselves, in refusing to concede to them what I regard as nothing but an elementary right. There is a certain amount of dockage in wheat no matter how excellent in quality it may be, and I do not think it is too much to ask that the millers should be allowed to mix with the screenings some amount of shorts to make it more acceptable to the market. I know that there are certain screenings that cannot be improved by any addition of bran or shorts, but there are others that possibly might be improved by the admixture, and I cannot see any objection to the permission to the millers so to mix their screenings, provided that the product is sold as soich. As I say, I am not advocating the cause of the millers and I merely put forward this suggestion with a view to eliciting the opinions of the committee. We are interested in seeing that justice is done everybody, and at the same time we want to be fair to ourselves.

I suppose this might be
called "renovated feed?"

I do not know.

Feeding Stuffs Act

I want to support the
minister in the proposal he makes. We must be fair to everyone and if the millers desire to turn out a certain grade of screenings I do not see that there can be any harm in their being permitted to add a certain amount of shorts so long as they label the article as screenings. The millers want to bring the stuff up to the market demands, and what the minister suggests is, I think, only fair.

I want to impress upon the minister as forcefully as I can the necessity when making regulations to insist that all screenings shall be ground as finely as possible. There are certain noxious weeds which are very small and are exceedingly difficult to grind. This is true particularly of mustard seed, and the regulations should provide that the grinding shall be so thorough as to preclude all possibility of these noxious weeds passing into the feed with the likelihood afterwards of germination.

I can see no necessity, from any sense of poetic or any other form of justice, for granting the request of the millers that they be allowed to mix shorts with their screenings. I have a long experience with the habits and methods of millers from the point of view of the purchaser and I am not a bit afraid that they will fall into bad financial waters through any such act. They are perfectly capable of taking care of themselves, and we need have no concern about them so far as this matter is concerned. This proposed adulteration will work out, as adulteration in all cases works out, in this way. The agent of the milling company comes along and says: "We have a nice line of stuff we call screenings at $20 a ton." The dealer says, "Well, that is a big price to ask for it because you don't pay anything for the stuff except the price of the sack and the filling of it." "Oh," he says, "but there is 50, 60, 70 per cent of shorts in it. While we call it screenings to comply with the law it is really mostly shorts, and the mixture is so much better." Now, no one will know exactly how much shorts the screenings will contain, because the percentage will not be marked on the sacks, and you will really buy a pig in a poke, as the saying is. The fact is that nobody will know what he is getting if this mixture is permitted, whereas if the screenings were sold by themselves the consumer could mix it to suit himself. Young pigs will require a different food from that which is given to older animals, and the main thing is to sell a pure article. This principle animated hon. members in discussing the question of oleomargarine. Hon. gentlemen were opposed
to any adulteration creeping into the manufacture of butter, and the same thing should apply here. There is no question whatever about justice in the matter; if the millers have bran to sell let them sell it as bran; if they have screenings to sell let it be so labelled. But do not allow any adulteration.

The hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) expressed the same opinion I hold in regard to noxious weeds. It is a well-known fact that in the grinding of mill feeds the smaller weed seeds are not crushed, especially mustard seed, with the result that they are capable of germination subsequently. I think that mustard seeds should be eliminated from the feeds. These seeds are a burden and an expense to the man who ships them and milling companies naturally look upon them as a nuisance unless they can be allowed to re-ship them in some other form. The Minister of Agriculture knows very well that to send these seeds back to the country is merely to intensify and perpetuate a menace. I think that the bill should provide at least that the percentage of these seeds that are included in mill feeds shall be stated. This principle was embodied in a bill which was discussed in the Agriculture committee on a former occasion, and I believe it is an important safeguard. With regard to the question of mixing bran and shorts in screenings, I think the sense of the committee is rather against the suggestion. If there is to be sold good shorts properly milled and kept dry I do not think there will be any difficulty in securing a good market for it.

To meet the consensus of opinion in the committee in regard to paragraph (c) of the resolution, I move that it be amended by striking out the word "pure" in the first line, and the words "shorts and mill screenings," and inserting after the word "flour" the words "or screenings," so that the paragraph will read:
-the bran, shorts, middlings, feed, flour or screenings meet the requirements, etc.
With regard to the matter raised by my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi, that is something that will be dealt with by regulation and we shall try to meet his views as far as possible.
Amendment agreed to.
I move that we strike out sub-paragraph (d) and paragraph 2, because they are contingent upon the first paragraph and can be dispensed with now. Then paragraph 3 will become paragraph 2.

Amendment agreed to.

Yes. -

Lake Grain Rates

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) spoke truly last evening when he said that this bill was one of paramount importance and should receive the careful consideration of the House. 9 p.m. At the outset I may say that I am entirely in accord with the action of the government in bringing forward this much-needed measure, and I extend to the government and to the hon. minister who is fathering the bill my congratulations for their courage in taking this step. Undoubtedly they are dealing with large and powerful interests that are dominated by prominent men in this country; they are dealing with a subject which must, as the minister himself said, present considerable difficulty so far as legislation bearing upon it is concerned. The people of Canada are to be 1 congratulated that the government, upon these matters being put before them, moved promptly and with despatch. It is courageous legislation, and the result of its enactment should be greatly beneficial to the people of western Canada in particular and to the people of Canada as a whole. The rates affecting the transport of the products of that part of our country which is far removed from its market, situated as it is in the centre of this wide continent-freight rates by rail and by lake- constitute one of the most important problems that we in the West have to deal with.
It is quite appropriate that the Liberal party, which broke the Canadian Pacific Railway monopoly by the effecting of the Crowsnest pass arrangement in 1897, an arrangement which was practically re-established last year, should, upon accession to power in these latter times, break the shipping monopoly that had fastened itself upon the people of western Canada. But the present government have gone further than that: During this session they have enacted an anti-combine bill, a measure that will enable those administering the criminal law to secure the necessary evidence in connection with any alleged combine. Under the criminal law as it existed the great difficulty was that you could not get the evidence, but under the anti-combine bill the evidence can be procured if a case exists. That, together with the bill that has just been passed enabling us to bring in legitimate competition against those who are dealing unfairly in the matter of privileges they enjoy under our shipping laws, should be ample protection, so far as the Great Lakes are concerned, to the producers of western Canada and should result in benefit to the whole Dominion.
There was appointed in February of this year, following the reports made to the government, a royal commission composed of three able men. Mr. Levi Thomson, a man who had lived for long years in western Canada, a man thoroughly familiar with the grain trade, a man who had had parliamentary experience and also was trained in the reception and weighing of evidence, was on that commission-undoubtedly a very suitable appointment. Mr. McLean was also there, a man with experience in dealing with rates; and Mr. Tremblay, a business man. Now, it was suggested last night in the course of the debate that this board should be composed of shippers who knew something of the shipping trade. That was not necessary at all, because the shipping interests were represented by the very ablest counsel that money could procure. All the facts that they could possibly present in their favour were laid before this commission. The government was represented by an able western counsel, a man of great experience in rate matters, a man whose practice for the last four or five years had been very wide in that particular field. That gentleman knew exactly where to go to get evidence, and how to bring it before the commission. So that, after all, it is not a question of the knowledge of the commissioners themselves. If you get fair-minded men, of moderate and reasonable view, men of sound and capable judgment, who can weigli and appraise the evidence brought before them by experts you make a judicious choice. In that respect the government selected, very wisely, an able commission, a commission against whom no charge of partiality could be advanced; and those hon. members who have read that commission's report will find that the statements made therein are moderate, reasonable, thoughtful and fair. There is in it nothing extreme, nothing unusual; the report is judicial in tone and judicial in language and thought.
Now, the story which the report of that commission unfolds is one of the most remarkable stories of trade and commerce ever told in this or any other country. The Great Lakes afford the only real outlet for our grain because the cost of transportation by rail is, as you all know', too high to permit it to be used entirely as a roadway for that grain. Some thirteen or fourteen years ago two enterprising young Duteh-Americans by the name of Wolvin, -who had had their training in the western United States and were operating from Duluth, came up into Canada and in company with one Norcross engaged in shipping on the Great Lakes. They gradually worked up a combination and this monopoly
Lake Grain Rates

became very strong. For thirteen years it grew stronger and stronger, and bolder and bolder as each year went by. Finally, apparently undaunted by anything, they imposed on the shippers and producers of western Canadi extortionate and unusual freight rates which culminated last year in discrimination against the very country that gave them its protection under its shipping rules. Finally there was created an organization which proceeded to intimidate its victims whom it compelled to take shipping space at its own rates over their own lakes. Like a leech or a weasel ;t fastened itself on the main artery of western Canada's trade and proceeded to bleed the West and the western producer slowly to death. Not only was that the prospect in sight, but there was even the likelihood of competing Canadian shipping being driven from our Great Lakes as Van Tromp the countryman of the Wolvins, once boasted he would drive British shipping from the seas.
The evidence shows that the method pursued by this company was to secure the cooperation of the Canada Steamships Limited. The Canada Steamships Limited was formed on the 17th June, 1913, with its head office in Montreal, and an authorized capital of $25,000,000. Among the directors we find the names of prominent men, at least one of whom is a member of this House, and another the head of the Canadian National Railways at this time.
Sir Henry Thornton is a director.

Yes, and R. M. Wol-vin, one of the individuals to whom I have alluded. There was formed in Winnipeg about the same time a company known as the Standard Shipping Company. The latter entered into an arrangement with the $25,000,000 company, the Canada Steamships Limited. This arrangement was most unusual in the shipping trade in the fact that it was reduced to writing. The purport of the contract was that this company, with headquarters in Winnipeg, was to have the sole right, so far as Canada Steamships Limited was concerned, to charter all space upon its vessels. In return for this it was to be given insurance placed upon all cargoes. These companies insisted that all grain shipped should be insured. There was an insurance company in the United States with whom every man in the West, who is shipping grain, was obliged to place his insurance, and this insurance was set at just twice the rate which could be obtained in other places. The loss incurred by all those who shipped grain .was very large. I think the United Grain Grow-
[ Mr. McMurray.]
ers last year claimed they lost $36,000 by being compelled to take this insurance; and the total loss in respect of all shippers ran into thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Do the grain shippers of the West simply insure their grain from Fort William to Montreal, or do they have a through rate from Winnipeg to Liverpoo1 or some other point on the other side?

My understanding is, the rate is from Fort William to the port on the lakes to which the grain is shipped. If it is going to Port Colborne the rate is to that place; if to Montreal the rate is to that port.
Why do they not get through insurance from Fort William to Liverpool?
The Standard Shipping Company, to which I have just referred will not permit them to do so.
What do you mean by the Standard Shipping Company?

The Standard Shipping Company is the company in Winnipeg which made this bargain with the Canada Steamships Limited that they would insure all the cargoes that were placed on board its vessels. Now, a singular thing in connection with this matter is, that before the contract would expire-I think it was to expire 1928 -it was renewed for another period of twelve years, so that it would not terminate until 1940, the full intention being that this monopoly that had been settled upon by the shippers of western Canada was to be continued for a long period of time. The commission found as a fact that a combination existed. They found that these various shipping companies on the lakes met in Toronto on the 4th of May and entered into what the commission found to be a combine. Then they met on the 8th May; and again on the 28th July they met in the city of New York. Their finding was that there was a combination. What did this combination do? They first exacted a tribute from the people of western Canada of double insurance on every cargo sent out. They discriminated against Canadian ports. They shipped from Fort William to Buffalo at a lower rate than they would ship from Fort William to the Georgian bay ports, although there was a difference in distance in favour of the Georgian bay ports of 316 miles. These rates were found to be actually fixed at the meeting to which I refer, and confirmed at a subsequent

Lake Grain Rates
meeting. Apparently all the shipping interests on those lakes were in this combination. We find them going so far that a grain buyer, I think it was in Chicago, declared that he would not be held up under these conditions at all, and proposed to charter a boat, to send it up to the head of the lakes, and bring down the grain independently of them. This proposal was met by a warning given to the shippers in Winnipeg that they would have difficulty in securing space for the shipment of grain. Probably it was not in those words, but to that effect. It would be interesting to read the summary of the findings of this commission. The first thing they find is as follows:
In the opinion of your commission a tacit understanding between these operators as to those rates existed during the whole season, and measures should be taken to prevent its continuation.
The second thing they found was:
Rates on grain between Canadian ports were discriminatory as compared with rates charged by Canadian operators on grain and other bulk freight between Canadian and United States ports, and as compared with those charged by American operators on grain and other bulk freight between United States ports.
It was contended by the shipping companies, as suggested by my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), in his illustrations before the House last night, that this discrimination might be caused by congestion in the ports, but in the fourth paragraph of the summary of the findings of the commission they say:
Congestion was as bad at Buffalo as at Port Col-borne, and was worse than at Bay ports; Therefore, discrimination cannot be justified by congestion.
Another contention set up by these shippers was that the advantage was with the American ports and that the vessels going in could operate at a lower rate on account of the fact that there was a return cargo

that was coal-going northwards; but the evidence showed that coal only constituted on this occasion some 22 per cent, and I think over a period of years some 29 per cent; so that all these vessels were coming back light, American as well as Canadian, and the concluding words of the commissioners were as follows:
It would seem, however, that in general, the advantage possessed by the American vessel in respect of coal is not so great as represented.
As an offset to that the commission state in paragraph 7 of their finding:
On the other hand, it has been admitted that labour costs were lower on the Canadian side than on the American.
They find these rates were unjustifiably high, and in paragraph 8 they say:
After making due allowance for additional cost of operating and handling to which the grain was subject, but which did not apply to ore and coal, there is still an excess of earnings from the transportation of grain between Canadian ports over earnings from the carriage of other bulk freight, which shows high and unjustifiable rates.
Then they say in paragraph 9:
The increase of the 1922 rates over those of 1921 by Canadian vessel operators was so great as to be high and unjustifiable.
Paragraph 11 reads:
The season of 1922 was characterized by high levets of rates which cannot but have been detrimental to all those engaged in the production and disposal of grain.
They found that it was injurious to the farmer who produced the grain, and the reason for that was forcibly explained yesterday by the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales). Paragraph 11 continues:
And it is therefore essential that through control of the upper levels of rates the competitive principle which has been relied upon by parliament in the case of water transportation should be permitted to be operative.
That is there must be free competition on the lakes. Paragraph 12 of the report reads:
The difficulties in the way of controlling rates on lake-borne grain are such that your commission is of the opinion that the only feasible method of rate control through a regulative tribunal is through maximum rates.
They have considered apparently, as they naturally would, all the possibilities of restoring competition among the shipping interests, and they came to the conclusion that the only possible release that could be given would be by the fixing of a maximum rate. They also suggest the power to suspend the coastal laws in respect to the grain trade be conferred upon the Governor in Council. It is suggested in this connection that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics should keep statistical records of the port cargoes in the coasting trade, such records to be based on returns from the vessel or vessel companies operating. As the bill was just put in my hands a short time ago, I do not know what provision there is for the suspending of these coastal laws. My own impression is that these coastal laws should be suspended on recommendation made to the government by the board or commission which deals with these rates. I believe that that would be a fair thing, because we are putting the control of this matter in the hands of an independent tribunal. We are giving them power independently of parliament to fix the

rates. Why should we not also give them power to lift the coastal shipping regulations. It is possible that we are lifting this matter as far as possible out of politics. It is said that we have lifted our railways out of the control of politics, in order that they may be fairly and properly operated in the interest of the people; and I submit that it would give satisfaction to the people of this country to feel that there was a tribunal independent of parliament, independent of the people and of these shipping companies, to deal with the question of the lifting of these coastal laws. It is in the interest of the government itself to prevent any criticism that might be fairly levelled against it through some misunderstanding on the part of the people of Canada, if they thought the coasting laws should not be lifted. A charge might be made against the government in the future, and the government be absolutely innocent. But if there is an independent body that has the confidence of all concerned in the country, that charge would not be levied against the government; the government would consequently be in a better position, and the people of Canada would be fully satisfied. I do not know whether that clause is in the bill or not; I have not read the bill; but speaking for myself, I would respectfully urge the minister and the government to give it consideration.
The commission points out the inequality of this insurance "hold-up." I use a common term, an opprobrious term, but that is the correct term to use. I am glad to see that the minister has inserted in his bill a drastic and strong provision, malting it prohibitive for a chartering broker to have anything to do at all with placing insurance. It was charged in our Banking committee not long ago that banks are interfering with the functions of insurance, and compelling people who placed their securities with them for loans, to insure through .them. That is absolutely unfair in this case. A man shipping his grain should have the right to go out into the market and to buy insurance in open competition if such can be had.
Some questions have been raised in connection with this bill by hon. members on this side of the House. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), last evening expressed a sentiment, that is no doubt believed in by many members on both sides of the House, when he enunciated the old doctrine of "laissez faire" of the Manchester School of economics, holding that legislation cannot ultimately correct; that the only corrective thing can be competition. I would remind my hon. friend that in the days
{Mr. McMurray.l
when the Manchester School flourished, England was reaching out for wider and wider markets, and competition existed in the effort to secure those wider markets. A great change has come over the economic world since then. Large combinations in restraint of trade have come into existence. The principle of watered stock now exists, and as regards practical measures, the doctrines of Cobden, Bright and John Stuart Mill are almost useless1 when it comes to devising an instrument curtailing monopolies that exist to-day. The condition is exceptional in that w'e have a monopoly, like that of the old German robber barons of the Rhine, who levied toll on all who passed up and down the river, controlling the single outlet for our grain, and I do not believe that if those members of the Manchester School were situated as the people of Canada are to-day they would contend that the doctrine of "laissez faire" applies or could apply. Can you tolerate licensed robbery under an economic doctrine of "laissez faire?"

Does the hon. member wish
to infer that there is watered stock in the Canada Steamships1 Company?
Does the hon. member suggest that there is not?
I did not. I was asking the hon. member.
If I suggested it?
Yes.

I made no suggestion
at all. I said simply that they had $25,000,000 worth of stock. My hon. friend can draw his own conclusions.
The second point made by the senior member for Halifax, was that he doubted the legality of this measure which we now are placing on the statute books. I gathered from his speech that he had two points, first, that this is not sound economics; second, that it is not legal. He did not state in what the illegality consisted, but I presume he thought it was an interference by the Dominion government with matters that were purely provincial. I do not think lake Superior or lake Huron is part and parcel of the province of Ontario. They are Dominion waters; they are international waters, and navigation, laws belong solely to the Dominion. I respectfully contend, because I have a very high opinion of my hon. friend's standing as a lawyer, that in this he is wrong. In my opinion if the government has jurisdiction anywhere, it is in regard to navigation on inland waters. I would go further and say that if there is any

doubt at all about the matter, we shall put the law into force and let the other fellow, the monopolist, fight it.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), feared that we could not fix rates from American ports to Canadian ports and vice versa. He seems to think, if I gathered his remarks correctly, that there was a danger of driving this shipping from Canada.
I am not affirming or denying whether that is correct or not. I did not make the argument or the deduction which my hon. friend makes.
Did he simply raise the query then, that that might happen?

I made the statement that we could not fix rates between a Canadian port and an American port, or between an American port and a Canadian port, and that that would affect the usefulness of the measure.

Then I misunderstood my hon. friend's argument. What we can do is this, we can fix rates that will be fair and reasonable. The tribunal appointed will, I submit, be composed of men of reputation for fairness and ability. They will probably have associated with them an efficient staff that will gather all data that is needed in order to arrive at a right and proper rate. I think the shipping interests need have no fear whatever that they will not receive at the hands of this properly-appointed tribunal, fair and proper treatment. If they are treated fairly and properly, there need be no fear of their discriminating against Canada. As a matter of fact, they cannot discriminate against Canada more than they have done already. Even if there is danger of their withdrawing from operation in Canada, there exists in this country a condition of affairs that no self-respecting government, when the facts are laid before them, can possibly tolerate any longer, and the government must act in the matter irrespective of consequences. The government must not be intimidated by any argument of that nature.
This combine that had the audacity to charge these terrific rates and to impose an illegal and altogether improper insurance on the shipper had the temerity to intimidate the people of Winnipeg. There is a series of interesting telegrams that passed between the members of this combine. They appear at page 19 of the report and I think that in all fairness to those who may come after us they should be placed on Hansard so that there may be no misapprehension if the subject
ever comes up again for discussion. These telegrams display the same intimidating attitude to those who had the courage to appeal to this government for protection against the injustice and the predatory measures practised against them. When one reads and carefully studies this report, when one ponders the evidence, one is appalled at the boldness of these men who secured control of the only shipping channel for our western grain. The name "Wolvin" is significant, and it is difficult for anyone to speak dispassionately and calmly as he realizes that significance in its fullest extent. The nearest synonym that I can suggest for it, if it has any English equivalent, would be the word "wolverine." The wolverine is described as a "voracious, sagacious and ferocious animal," and apparently these men exhibited all these qualities, because they were certainly voracious, they were undoubtedly sagacious, and to the shippers of western Canada they were beyond any question "ferocious." Hon. members will realize the audacity of this whole matter when they read the telegrams that were exchanged, as disclosed in this report. Mr. Emderby, of the Canada Steamship Lines, despatched the following message to Mr. L. H. Wolvin, the man handling the Standard Steamship Companies in Winnipeg which collected this illegal insurance. The telegram is dated September 27, 1922:
Better get those instructions to Winnipeg in writing about booking no more cargoes until this coasting law question settled. Our agreement was now (no?) new business. Make your instructions to them absolutely definite.
That is to say, if the government delayed in settling this coasting law question they would hold up the entire grain movement at . the head of the lakes. On September 15, 1922, the following telegram was sent:
L. H. Wolvin, Esq.,
Central Shipping Co.,
Postal Telegraph Bldg.,
Chicago, 111.
We are not chartering any more Canadian boats for September loading. Think it best to clean up what we have and if we have open space we can get pretty nbarly whatever we ask for it. We are doing some October but thought perhaps we had better hold off on this also except with Sid Smith he is figuring half million lastaff abstract which we should supply him and then raise rate. Answer.
W. W. Hall.
This man had to get his grain out on the market and he started to curry favour with these shipping barons; so he was to be given an opportunity of getting his half million out before the rates were raised. On October 3, we find the following telegram from the same man, Hall:
Lake Grain Rates

L. H. Wolvin, Esq.,
c/o R. A. & W. M. Williams,
Kirby Bldg.,
Cleveland, Ohio.
Hope you are able to advise us soon with regard to ore and want to point out to you that before taking care of O'Donahue we had better take care of Sid Smith who was first to wire Minister of Marine this morning at length explaining situation as it really is with regard to shipping, and he is as badly in need of tonnage to fill his sales as any other shipper in the building and will be in very bad hole if we cannot help him out on some grain on or before tenth. He just showed the difference between willingness to help us and careless attitude that most of others had.
W. W. Hall.
All this occurred in Canada, and it is nothing but straight intimidation. These people dared to punish those who would not openly advocate the rates under which they themselves were operating.

Does not my hon. friend believe that people who own shipping should have a right to barter in the market for the highest possible price for their commodity, and if they refuse to accept any other than their own price should they be compelled to do so? In other words, ought not the matter to be regulated by the law of supply and demand?

In open competition,
yes; but not under combines, which are illegal.
Where has any combine been proven?
If the hon. member had been listening to me for the last forty minutes he would agree, I think, that it has been absolutely proven.
I should like the hon. gentleman to state in two or three words where there has been proved to be a conspiracy .1 restraint of trade.

The hon. gentleman
evidently has not read the report of the com-rmssion. If he has, then his memory is foggy.
Not in the least.

The very first paragraph in the summary states that there was a combine:
-and in the opinion of your commission a tacit understanding between these operators as to those rates existed during the whole season, and measures should be taken to prevent its continuation.
I have not found that there was a combine; the tribunal appointed to consider the question unanimously decided that there was.
Who were the practical shipping men on the commission?
I went into that question before the hon. member came in.
I am not trying to offer any factious opposition.

There is one more telegram I want to put on record. On October 11, 1922, there was a telegram from L. H. Wolvin, Cleveland, Ohio, to W. W. Hall, Winnipeg, as follows:
OKay Smith's Bay charter. Keep this strictly confidential. Do not want to offer Stewart anything just now account of Ottawa. Where can I telegraph Stewart?
Stewart was the man in Winnipeg who had the courage and the backbone to protest against this combine and to appeal to the government for protection. Smith, who was the first to wire tire Minister of Marine, was to have protection; he was to be taken care of by these concerns. But Stewart, the manly man, the man who had the courage to stand up and fight for himself as a man should, was to be punished. I should like to see the telegram that Sid Smith sent to the Minister of Marine.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is disclosed in this very brief report, which is evidently written by reasonable and fair-minded men, such an appalling condition of affairs as I do not think has ever before existed either in this country or in the United States. No school of economics can justify this abuse or apply a remedy; parliament itself must intervene. Who is going to compete against this gigantic organization known as the Canada Steamships Company with its S25,000,000 capital in ships? One company that did try in Winnipeg was intimidated and told it could not get space. The head of that company, rich and wealthy though he was, and a powerful magnate in the United States, could not get his grain down the lakes, and I presume he had either to cancel his contract or take space at the rates dictated by the combination. Where such a combination is in absolute control, and there can be no competition, can any hon. member seriously and honestly argue, whether he be committed to the policy of free trade and the doctrine of the Manchester School -and I believe in it very strongly myself, but I recognize that changing conditions have modified its applicability and, indeed, made it impossible of application, such as when strong forces absolutely shut out competition [DOT]-can any hon. member contend for a moment that the government should not intervene? I do not think so, I feel confident that he will agree with me in my submission that the government must take action. In the United States government control is exer-

cised on the regular routes by virtue of the Alexander Act, which is referred to in this report. Even with this limited jurisdiction the commission finds that competition is kept alive on the American side, but it found no evidence of any competition on the Canadian side.
I congratulate the government upon having the courage to introduce legislation that will,
I believe, curb these great and powerful interests, prevent their again exacting extortionate rates from our shippers in the West, and put an end to the discrimination which those interests have exercised against our ports in favour of American ports. I do not think that this legislation will drive our grain away from its natural outlet down the St. Lawrence river to Montreal and Quebec. It is undoubtedly in the interests of western Canada, as well as of Montreal and Quebec, it is undoubtedly in the interests of all people, including our millers, that this combine should be broken. I do not think that we may have to deal with it harshly. I think that the publicity which will attend the work of investigation and examination by the Grain Commission, coupled with the power of suspending the coasting laws, will effectually curb this combine without inflicting any injury upon it.
I feel that criminal proceedings should be taken against these men who have so flagrantly and audaciously defied the laws of this country-the very laws that gave them protection and enabled them to operate their business. When the labouring men of Canada were charged with illegally combining-as happened in western Canada a few years ago -the Dominion government did not hesitate to invade the jurisdiction of the province of Manitoba and insist upon their trial. I think this Liberal government should deal feat-lessly with large interests, no matter how powerful they may be, in the same way a3 they deal with the humblest citizen in the land when occasion demands it. The question came up last night as to where the jurisdiction lay for prosecution. As was properly stated by the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), the criminal law of Canada is administered by the provinces. I believe that the criminal prosecution undertaken in Winnipeg by the Dominion government serveral years ago was a most unusual invasion of the provincial field and was done under the War Measures Act. This government to-day cannot come into the province and prosecute this combine without invading provincial rights. The province of Manitoba has full jurisdiction to arraign its citizens for misdemeanours against the state, a jurisdiction which is common to all the provinces, and would not tolerate any invasion of its jurisdiction by the Dominion authorities. It would be a breach of the constitution for the Dominion government to attempt such invasion. In a word, while we desire to punish T,hese men severely, we must ourselves respect the law of the land. But there is nothing to hinder the government laying criminal charges against these men in the proper courts of Manitoba, and then it rests with the attorney general of the province to proceed. I am sure that so far as western Canada is concerned, the attorneys general would co-operate with the Minister of Justice in any criminal proceedings that may be considered advisable.
I think the men forming this oppressive combine should be dealt with under the criminal law. Such a course would be a step towards wiping out this stain on Canada's honour. And I am confident that the men in question would receive a fair trial in our criminal courts. I am also confident that the passing of this legislation wall ensure fair treatment of our shipping interests. Therefore I am strongly in favour of the bill with the exception which I have mentioned.

The part of Canada particularly interested in this bill is the agricultural part, the part adapted to the growing of grain and the raising of live stock-an ever-growing industry. Agriculture on any considerable scale commenced only with the advent of the railroad somewhere about 1885. Since that time the agriculturist in that part of the Dominion has had a continuous fight against the protected interests of this country. We have practically no industrial concerns in western Canada, and the organized interests of eastern Canada have taken advantage of our position in that regard, with the result that all the earnings of our people have gone east and have not been used for our benefit; the greater our earnings have been the greater has been the bondage we have laboured under. I say now the time has come when we can no longer stand the elimination of competition among all with whom we have to do in the way of distribution of commodities, the public utilities, and so on. The lake freight question is only one of others, but it is a case in point to show how our position has been taken advantage of; it is a marked factor in increasing the cost of production to a point where we can no longer compete with our products in the world's markets. Two or three years ago one of our farmers' companies, in an effort to keep down the cost, tried to go into the export business for at least a part of their grain, but we found ourselves up against one of the most complete and ruinous combines that ever existed in this country as regards shipping and insurance on the Great Lakes. It was not until the last crop moving season that the situation became unbearable.
